Female Patagonian flounder (Paralichthys patagonicus) attain a maximum total length of 48 centimeters [Li = 48 centimeters], a size that is relatively modest compared to some larger congeners inhabiting the North Atlantic. This ultimate length is achieved through a prolonged growth trajectory that extends across much of the species' lifespan. At a stable water temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C], hatched yolk-sac larvae emerge from the chorion following an incubation period of approximately 4 days [ab = approximately 4 days]. These lecithotrophic prolarvae, which measure only a few millimeters in total length, carry a substantial yolk reserve that sustains them during the brief endotrophic phase before mouth opening and the onset of exogenous feeding. The wet weight of newly emerged larvae is estimated at 0.00056 grams [Wwb = 0.00056 grams], a value derived from egg diameter measurements in a related species and reflecting the diminutive starting point from which somatic growth proceeds. This neonatal mass is among the smallest recorded for flatfishes of comparable adult size, highlighting the dramatic scope of ontogenetic mass gain required to reach the adult body plan.

The total length at which female Patagonian flounder first attain puberty has been determined to be 33.5 centimeters [Lp = 33.5 centimeters], a size that typically corresponds to an age of between two and three years under natural thermal regimes. The wet weight at puberty, calculated from the length-weight relationship established for this population, is 287 grams [Wwp = 287 grams], representing a substantial fraction of the species' maximum body mass. By contrast, the ultimate wet weight achieved by fully grown females can reach approximately 875 grams [Wwi = approximately 875 grams], a figure derived from allometric scaling of length data and indicating that post-pubertal somatic growth continues well beyond the onset of reproductive maturity. This pattern of continued mass accumulation after puberty is common among iteroparous teleosts and allows females to allocate increasing resources to fecundity as they age. The gonadosomatic index (GSI), measured under controlled conditions at 17 °C [T = 17 °C], reached 4% [GSI = 4%] during the spawning season.

The lifespan of Patagonian flounder under natural conditions, based on otolith-based age estimates from wild-caught specimens maintained at 17 °C [T = 17 °C], extends to approximately 13 years [am = approximately 13 years]. This longevity is consistent with the slow life-history pace typical of many large-bodied flatfishes inhabiting temperate continental shelf waters. Individuals achieve this maximum age by balancing the energetic demands of reproduction against the maintenance costs of a benthic predatory lifestyle. The relationship between body size and age reveals that female ultimate total length of 48 centimeters [Li = 48 centimeters] is typically attained near the end of the second decade of life, with growth rates slowing considerably after the onset of sexual maturity. Comparative data from congeners suggest that this lifespan is near the upper range for Paralichthys species, possibly reflecting the relatively cool, productive waters of the Patagonian shelf that support slow but sustained growth over many years without imposing excessive metabolic costs.

Reproductive output in female Patagonian flounder is closely tied to body size and age. Gravid individuals produce multiple batches of pelagic eggs over an extended spawning season, with fecundity scaling positively with both length and mass. The wet weight at puberty of 287 grams [Wwp = 287 grams] marks the threshold above which females first participate in spawning events, though first-time spawners typically contribute fewer oocytes than older, larger conspecifics. As females approach their ultimate wet weight of 875 grams [Wwi = 875 grams], fecundity per spawning event increases considerably, reflecting the greater abdominal cavity volume available for ovarian development. Field surveys indicate that the gonadosomatic index peaked at 4% [GSI = 4%] during the austral summer, coinciding with the period of maximum water temperature and primary productivity at a temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C].

The early life history of Patagonian flounder is characterized by rapid developmental transitions during the first days post-hatching. At the experimental temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C], yolk-sac larvae complete the absorption of endogenous reserves and commence exogenous feeding approximately 4 days [ab = approximately 4 days] after eclosion, a critical period during which mortality rates are highest due to the risk of starvation before successful prey capture. The diminutive larval wet weight of 0.00056 grams [Wwb = 0.00056 grams] underscores the vulnerability of this early stage to environmental stochasticity. Following metamorphosis, juveniles settle to the benthos and begin the slow accumulation of somatic tissue that will eventually yield the adult form. The maximum lifespan of 13 years [am = 13 years] is thought to be facilitated by this prolonged juvenile phase, which allows individuals to buffer against years of poor recruitment by delaying maturity when conditions are unfavorable at a temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C]. Such life-history flexibility is a common feature of flatfishes inhabiting variable shelf environments.
